episode_title: Defense Innovation Unit with Maj Gen Joseph "Solo" Kunkel

real_qa.q: What are the three Mission Areas in Air Force force design and how do they differ in operational capability requirements?
real_qa.r: Mission Area 1 involves close-in unmanned capabilities that operate in contact with adversaries from sanctuary positions. Mission Area 2 encompasses pulsed operations of fighters, bombers, and destroyers with medium-range effects. Mission Area 3 involves large-scale force flows that take a month or more to deploy and persist in theater. The framework distinguishes capabilities needed across different global regions and threat environments, where Mission Area 1 requires small, mobile systems with limited signatures to survive in contested environments.

real_qa.q: How much cheaper are Collaborative Combat Aircraft compared to manned fighters in terms of cost differential?
real_qa.r: Collaborative Combat Aircraft can be procured for three to four times less cost than manned fighters. This cost difference enables either purchasing a fighter fleet for significantly less money, or buying significantly more fighters for the same amount of money, with a certain portion being unmanned. However, CCAs are positioned as extensions of existing capabilities operating from large infrastructure rather than edge force systems.
real_qa.requete: Collaborative Combat Aircraft cost comparison manned fighters

real_qa.q: What is the adaptation cycle timeline difference between the Autonomous Warfare Command and current military combatant commands?
real_qa.r: The Autonomous Warfare Command is being built for adaptation cycles measured in days, weeks, and months, versus current combatant commands that adapt on scales of years and decades. For example, the F-22 took 20 years to field after identifying enemy radar capabilities, but new autonomous capabilities must be developed and integrated into the force very quickly to remain effective against rapidly evolving threats.
real_qa.requete: Autonomous Warfare Command adaptation cycle timeline

real_qa.q: What are the four main capability areas that Defense Innovation Unit structures its work around for future warfare?
real_qa.r: DIU has structured itself around four likely problem-solution sets: long-range kill chains or kill webs, autonomous systems, the 10X portfolio (defined as faster, cheaper, better capabilities produced in mass), and artificial intelligence. The organization focuses on these capability areas when reaching out to services and combatant commands to support their force designs.
real_qa.requete: Defense Innovation Unit DIU four capability areas strategy

real_qa.q: What is the relationship between Defense Innovation Unit, the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned, and the Autonomous Warfare Command in the acquisition structure?
real_qa.r: DIU develops and tests capabilities through the Drone Dominance Program gauntlets, which DERPM-UXS will adopt for its acquisition framework. Within a year, DERPM will be completely integrated into the Autonomous Warfare Command as part of it. DERPM will work on behalf of Autonomous Warfare Command for buying unmanned systems, while DIU continues developing and competing capabilities—described as a nesting doll configuration where eventually they will all be one.
real_qa.requete: DIU DERPM Autonomous Warfare Command acquisition structure relationship

guest.titre: Military Deputy to the Defense Innovation Unit
guest.bio_context: Major General Joseph Solo Kunkel is a fighter pilot with experience flying F-15s and F-22s who conducted operational planning and wargaming for the Air Force before joining DIU. Over the last five years, his Air Force roles led him to develop expertise in the acquisition process and force design, positioning him to bridge operational military needs with innovation procurement at the Defense Innovation Unit.

real_quote: We're not getting things in the hands of warfighters. If you want to get things in the hands of warfighters, you need to focus on the operational problems that warfighters have.
key_stats: Collaborative Combat Aircraft cost: three to four times less than manned fighters

Long-range one-way attack drone development: created in a garage and produced at significantly lower cost than Tomahawk cruise missiles developed over decades

transcript_full: Welcome to Acquisition Talk, a podcast on how the military buys and fields capabilities. I'm your host, Eric Lofgren. You can find more at acquisitiontalk.com. Thanks for listening. Major General Joseph Solo Kunkel is the military deputy to the Defense Innovation Unit, and before that, he did operational planning and wargaming for the Air Force and flew F-15s and F-22s. Solo, thanks for joining me on Acquisition Talk. Hey, my pleasure. So you're not an acquisition guy by trade. How does your thinking about the operational problems in the Pacific kind of pull you into this work? I'm not an acquisition guy by trade, but in the last five years, the jobs I've held within the Air Force have led me down this path where I have an understanding of the acquisition process. And, you know, we're in a new era where we actually need new capabilities. We have a set of capabilities that were developed in the 1980s. the capabilities we need for the future are not those capabilities that were introduced in the Reagan era. So that requires a knowledge and understanding of the acquisition process. So we know exactly what it takes to get these new things that we have to build. And so can you walk through this concept of mission areas one, two, three? How did that framing come about? Yeah, that framing came about about two years ago. The Air Force isn't using it right now in their force design. But when we were thinking about what was uniquely different about the capabilities that we needed to procure, to field, to solve operational problems for combatant commanders, there wasn't this really neat way to describe the different types of capabilities. If you go back to coming out of the Vietnam era, the capabilities that we developed then were for a very specific problem. They were for a Soviet Union problem. And we developed all these capabilities that we currently operate for that Soviet Union problem. And our thought was, and it was proven out by a lot of analysis in Wargaming, was that we didn't just need a universal set of capabilities. We needed capabilities that could operate in different parts of the globe under different threats. And that required this distinction between capabilities that were coming from over the horizon and operating from sanctuary and providing long-range effects. And it also required a distinction of the attributes of the capabilities that would be operating from in close within a contested area in contact with the adversary. So that Mission Area 1, 2, 3 was simply a construct for us to identify and clarify the different sets of attributes that new capabilities would need to fight in this new environment. Yeah, so my understanding was like Mission Area 1 was the close-in kind of unmanned stuff that you could proliferate in high volume, but it can't come from far, so it needs to be based pretty close. Then you got Mission Area 2, which is like the pulsed operations of fighters, bombers, and destroyers, potentially similar types of capabilities. And then 3 was like the whole tip fit of I'm flowing. It's going to take a long time, maybe a month or more, but I'm going to flow large scale forces to persist in the theater. It seems like the other services had similar concepts like the Navy has its tailored forces now. Was this kind of aligning? How did you think about all the other services and what you were doing versus the other services? Yeah, we built this framework and then I took it over to my other service buddies and said, hey, what do you think about this? And they were like, wow, this is really good. This describes what we are trying to do. Interestingly, the Navy was like, yeah, we want to do all of these. That describes us perfectly. And then the Marine Corps was like, yeah, that describes us, but we only want to do this Missionary One stuff, this stuff that's in contact. And the Army was about the same. And interestingly, what I found was that the Air Force needed to employ a range of capabilities to support its mission. It couldn't just do these long range things. It couldn't just do medium range things. It also had to do short range things as well. And those short range things were the things that were fundamentally new. They were fundamentally different. We hadn't done those. And I felt like the long range kill change and that even though it's different and it's hard because it's going to require some long range sensing, I felt like that was a natural evolution of the current force we had. So that leads us to this Missionary One, I think what's now called the Edge Force. So where does collaborative combat aircraft kind of fit into this picture? Is that a Missionary One thing or is it more of an extension of the traditional force just unmanned? Yeah, so that's a great question. And that's where the construct of three sets of forces really comes in handy to distinguish these types of things. The CCA, even though it's autonomous, It's going to be an extension of the things that already exist. When I look at why you would want to do a CCA versus a manned fighter, a lot of it comes down to cost. You can do a CCA for significantly cheaper than what you can do with manned fighters. And I think the cost of our fighters is publicly available information. I think the cost of CCAs is publicly available. and what you'll find is three to four times is the cost difference between the two. So you can either, one, buy a fighter fleet for significantly less money, or two, buy significantly more fighters for the same amount of money. It's just a certain number that's just going to be unmanned. And so that's where I think about CCA. It's not in this MA-1. The key distinction is that it's not operating within this contested environment. I think largely, except for a couple of concepts that exist, It's going to be operating from large infrastructure, large fuel facilities, large weapons storage facilities, those types of things. So can you describe maybe some of the capabilities that the Air Force is fielding or buying or investing in for this Mission Area 1 stuff? It seems that the kind of Group 1 through 3 UAVs is more relegated to Air Force special operations. Is that right? Is that like a natural home for it? Rather than speak specifically for the Air Force, I'd rather talk about the Joint Force. That's where DIU sits. But when you look at the long range one way attack or one way attack drones that we need to procure to do missions of the services and fundamentally new ways. We haven't spent a lot of time doing that yet. But I would suggest to your original question, these things can't be like a special operations bolt on. They can't just be like, yeah, we're going to bolt this new force onto this stuff that exists, and they'll be separate and distinct from them. It's got to be completely integrated into the force. And when I talk to combatant commanders, that's what they want. They want capabilities that are completely integrated. So when they develop CONOPS, they have this understanding of how you make them work in coordination with and synchronized with these other capabilities that already exist. and that's frankly when we've done this in war games that becomes the magic sauce it's the integration of the capabilities not just one set of capabilities alone so do you think uh like from a service perspective for these unmanned capabilities there needs to be one centralized force generation activity for that or do you think because currently a lot of the unmanned stuff can fit into across different verticals or you could have air mobility you could have strike on the Navy side, you could have surface, underwater air. So should it be aggregated or do you think of this as more like, hey, each kind of force generation activity or command should have its own unmanned and not a single thing? I think it depends on the service. For the Army and the Marine Corps, I would think that they would want those integrated into the formations that they already have. So their infantry capabilities, you'd think that those would, it would fundamentally change how infantry operates. But for instance, if you go back to the Navy operating surface vessels, I don't envision a world where you have a bunch of unmanned things that are like in a surface unit or a bunch of unmanned subsurface things that are integrated into a submarine unit. In the Air Force, I think it's the same thing. The Air Force has fighters, they have bombers, they have cargo aircraft, etc. And I think what you would find is these edge capabilities for the Air Force, you would find them operating in their own units. So it depends. So the fourth generation model, I think, is going to depend on service. How about for the larger stuff like the Group 5 UAVs for example in the Navy they already thinking about doing that through the carrier model and like maybe the CCAs through air combat command Do you think those bigger things that are outside the DIRPOM, UXS, the direct reporting program manager for unmanned, you think those things still live with the big man stuff or not? Or does it depend if they're going to work on a manned unmanned teaming? I do. I think those capabilities can be described by their attributes. And when we get to what's going to be under the DERP and UXS, it's going to be these edge force capabilities, the things that are not dependent on large surface vessels like aircraft carriers to deploy, that are not dependent on large fixed bases, that are capable of operating from remote areas, unimproved areas, these areas that are still under threat that are contested. But the fundamental difference in this set of capabilities is they're small enough, mobile enough, they have limited signatures, that they make really, really hard targets. And that becomes the distinctive feature of this set of capabilities. It's not that they're unmanned. It's not that they're autonomous. I think we're going to see autonomy and unmanned becomes something that's just normal. The distinction with this set of capabilities is that it's in contact with the adversary. And so you've got to think differently about how they survive and generate combat power. And we've got to think differently about the fourth generation model and employment construct. Most of the capabilities we have right now are dependent on this thing called the TIPFID or the deployment of forces into a theater. and this assumption that we're going to have time to get them into theater before the fight starts. And the problem with that assumption is that many of the things we have, they're just too darn big to posture forward. So in order for things to be immediately employable and not be dependent on this tip-fit, they're going to have to be smaller, they're going to have to be cheaper, and many of the large things, even if they're unmanned, won't satisfy that criteria. So that's where I think the distinction is. So if these things are smaller, they don't have the endurance or the range, what does that mean from kind of a partners or basing? Where do we store them? Is this completely dependent on our allies and partners being on board with having our systems forward? Or how do you think about that? Yeah, just writ large. I think to a greater extent than we've ever had before, our forces, our force generation model is going to be more dependent on posture. The ability to posture things forward and leave things forward. You can't do that with a wing of F-35s or multiple wings of F-35s. And you've seen us do it in small numbers to have like this vanguard force that was there in place and ready to go when the fight started. But we always depend on bringing more forces into theater. I think with this set of capabilities, posture, being able to have many of them forward is going to be much more important. So, yeah, to your point, it will require a much closer relationship with our allies and partners in regions that are forward. But the goodness of that is these capabilities will be immediately employable. So immediately employable and persistent become the hallmarks of capabilities for the future, particularly in this set of capabilities. There's a pretty famous memo that just came out on Autonomous Warfare Combatant Command. It seems to imply that unmanned is a unique competency. So how do you think about Autonomous Warfare Command? What's it going to do in your mind? Unmanned or autonomous service, we looked at maybe we just start within the services, and then we looked at a combatant command and there was not like a really solid fit where you could compare what we wanted to do to something that already existed and the closest that we had was this functional combatant command so that is what we went with but i think this thing will look different than the combatant commands that we have and the thing that's unique about it is the fact that it's going to be built for adaptation adaptation becomes the key for this set of capabilities because what worked two weeks ago may not work today and you're going to have to change it you're going to have to adapt it not only do you adapt the capability but in many cases the tactics and the doctrine will have to change as well so we're building in this autonomous warfare command a command or a unit that is capable of adapting and being on an adaptation cycle that is measured in days, weeks, and months versus what we currently have is the adaptation cycle responds to these large changes in the operational environment and then adapts on the scale of years and decades. You can see that played out. F-22 responded to changes in the environment. We thought we needed a new fighter. It was clear that the enemy was going with a certain radar band, So we built a capability that was perfectly matched for that. But it took us 20 years to feel the thing where this set of capabilities we know has to be developed very quickly and integrated into the force very quickly. So that adaptation cycle is what becomes unique about it. So what's the relationship in your understanding between future autonomous warfare combatant command, the direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned, and then defense innovation unit? How do all of these capabilities stack up, like, when we get to full operational capability? Yeah, so we're building this thing up right now, and we are using the pieces of the puzzle that we have. We know that we need to build a command that has this really high adaptation cycle, so that's going to be fundamentally new. And we've stood up an operational planning team that's going to work that, and they'll figure out exactly what that combatant command entity needs to look like. We also know that we've got to continue buying unmanned systems, and that's where the DERPM steps in. I think what you'll see is within a year, the DERPM is going to be completely integrated into this Autonomous Warfare Command. It'll just be part of it. And then DIU's relationship in this, the Drone Dominance Program was stood up within DIU. And so we've got really vast experience in how we develop, how we bring companies in, how we test, how we compete these capabilities and these things we've called gauntlets. And that's been very successful. And the DERPM wants to adopt that framework for testing and developing and acquiring these types of capabilities. So that is where DIU falls in. And DIU is going to be working on behalf of the DERPM to bring capabilities together, to run the gauntlets, to do those types of things. And then the DERPM will be working for the Autonomous Warfare Command when it stands up. It's kind of a nesting doll configuration. Eventually, they'll all be one. So do you think of DIU as like an acquisition arm, someone that goes out and experiments, prototypes? and they're kind of a similar arm as maybe DERPM-RAZ in the Navy or some of these other program offices in the Army and the Air Force that will actually do some of the work, but DERPM-UXS and Autonomous Warfare Combatant Command are orchestrating it, or do you think they're pulling more of those acquisition authorities in-house on behalf of the services? I think it's too early to tell exactly how it's going to land. I do know that the service is standing up these new capabilities. I think that's just all goodness and all a good move. How we end up splitting the acquisition authorities, what that looks like, I think that's still TBD. But what we do know is that the DERPM will have to have acquisition authorities that are unlike most combatant commands. I think it'll look similar to SOCOM and the OT&E type function or service-like responsibilities that SOCOM has. But again, to what we talked about earlier, I think these are capabilities that need to be institutionalized. They need to be integrated in every formation. And that means you need decisive mass. And if we just maintain this SOCOM model, we won't get the decisive mass. We'll just get the unique capabilities, but they won't be integrated in the rest of the service like we need them to be. That's why I think there's going to be a huge dependence on the services for this so we can get them integrated fully, not just a bolt-on capability. One of the things that we saw in the Senate's version of Autonomous Warfare Combatant Command was the test and evaluation authorities. So it seems DAU has done a great job with the gauntlets for drone dominance. Are you guys expecting to expand that out for all different types of capabilities that you working on and delivering that as something of an OT kind of service to the Autonomous Warfare Command and DERPM UXS Yeah absolutely I think what you see in the coming months is the release of gauntlets in a much greater span of capabilities We'll be doing gauntlets for surface vessels. We'll be doing for subsurface vessels. We'll do it for longer range capabilities. That model seems to have worked. And so we're going to amplify it. So let's step back a second. How did you actually end up in the military deputy position at DIU? Oh, wow. Yeah, interesting question. So Owen West, who was just a fantastic individual, just an amazing guy and completely committed to our military, is someone that I've been collaborating with for a number of years. He was in Doge while I was doing Air Force design, and he thought the Air Force was doing things well. To this day, he will say that the Air Force did DOGE and took the DOGE mission seriously about how to cut back and scale back. He says we did it better than any other service. But he found out he was going to go be the director of DIU, and he asked me to join him. He's like, Solo, you need to join me on this team. And I'm like, what do you want me to do? And he said, hey, we're not transitioning capabilities. We're not getting things in the hands of warfighters. And I'm like, okay, if you want to get things in the hands of warfighters, you need to not focus on the tech. You need to focus on the operational problems that warfighters have. And he's like, well, that sounds pretty good. We focus on operational problems. And he brought me on board to do that, to get closer to the services, to get closer to the combatant commands, and then help them innovate, help them procure capabilities that sometimes it's hard to do. It's hard. The system we've built makes it really hard to do innovative things just by how we do money, how we do requirements, how we do acquisition. It's all built to do these slow things over generations, not fast, very quick in timeframes that are like within the budget year. And so he brought me in to help identify operational problems and help us transition capabilities. So I'm having a blast. It's a great organization, and we are moving fast. On the operational problems issue, JASIDS is dead, but long live JASIDS within the services to some degree.
